11680:
"Out of whack" means that something is not working properly, not in its correct state, or not in the right balance. It describes anything that has gone wrong, become misaligned, broken down, or stopped functioning the way it should.

Think of a clock. When every gear is in its right place and working smoothly, the clock ticks perfectly. But if one gear slips out of position, the whole clock goes wrong — the hands move too fast, too slow, or not at all. That clock is "out of whack."

The idiom works for machines, bodies, systems, relationships, schedules — almost anything that can go wrong or become unbalanced.

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand what "whack" means here — because it is not being used in its everyday sense of "a hard hit."

In older American English, "whack" also meant proper working order or correct condition. So:

  • "In whack" = working correctly, properly aligned, in good shape
  • "Out of whack" = no longer in that good condition; broken, misaligned, or unbalanced

The phrase "in whack" is almost never used today on its own, but its opposite — "out of whack" — survived and became very common.

The idiom originated in American English in the late 1800s. It is believed to come from the idea of craftsmen and workers physically striking or knocking something into proper shape or alignment (like a carpenter hammering a joint into place). When a thing had been properly knocked into shape, it was "in whack." When it slipped out of that alignment, it was "out of whack."

Over time, the phrase moved far beyond physical objects and began applying to anything that feels off, broken, or imbalanced.

1. Physical Objects and Machines

When a machine, tool, device, or mechanism is broken or not functioning correctly.

  • "The printer is out of whack again — it keeps jamming every few pages."
  • "Something in the car engine is out of whack. I can hear a strange noise."
  • "The fan blades are out of whack. One of them is bent."

2. The Human Body

When a part of your body is in pain, injured, stiff, or not functioning as it should. This is one of the most common uses.

  • "I slept in a bad position and now my neck is completely out of whack."
  • "My back went out of whack after I lifted those heavy boxes."
  • "Her knee has been out of whack since the accident last year."

3. Internal Body Systems and Health

When something inside your body — like hormones, blood sugar, digestion, or sleep — is imbalanced or irregular.

  • "My sleep schedule is totally out of whack this week. I keep waking up at 3 a.m."
  • "His blood pressure has been out of whack for months."
  • "All this stress has thrown my digestive system out of whack."

4. Abstract Systems and Plans

When a plan, schedule, budget, system, process, or organisation is no longer working properly or has become unbalanced.

  • "The company's finances are out of whack. They are spending far more than they earn."
  • "My whole schedule went out of whack when the first meeting ran two hours late."
  • "The tax system in this country is completely out of whack."

5. Relationships and Dynamics

When a balance between two people, groups, or forces has been disturbed.

  • "Their work-life balance is totally out of whack. He works sixteen hours a day."
  • "The power dynamic in that relationship is out of whack."

6. Numbers, Data, and Figures

When numbers, statistics, or measurements seem wrong, don't match up, or are far off from what they should be.

  • "These calculations are out of whack. The total doesn't add up at all."
  • "The poll results look out of whack compared to what every other survey found."

This is an informal, everyday idiom. You would use it in:

  • Casual conversation with friends or family
  • Informal writing (text messages, emails to colleagues you know well)
  • Informal spoken settings at work

You would generally avoid it in:

  • Formal writing (academic papers, official reports)
  • Formal speeches or presentations

It is primarily American English, but it is widely understood in other English-speaking countries as well.

The idiom can describe anything from a minor inconvenience to a serious breakdown — the context tells you how bad it is.

  • "My coffee machine is out of whack" — probably a small annoyance
  • "His entire nervous system is out of whack" — sounds serious

The phrase itself does not specify the severity; that comes from the words around it.

These idioms and phrases carry a similar meaning:

  • Out of order — something is broken or not functioning (also used for inappropriate behaviour)
  • On the fritz — a machine is broken or malfunctioning
  • Off-kilter — something is tilted, unbalanced, or not quite right
  • Off balance — something has lost its proper equilibrium
  • Not right — simple, plain version of the same idea
  • Broken — the most direct word, though "out of whack" often implies something subtler than complete breakage

"Out of whack" does not always mean something is completely broken. Often, it means something is slightly off, misaligned, or not functioning as smoothly as it should. It sits somewhere between "perfectly fine" and "completely broken."

For example:

  • "The door hinges are out of whack" — the door probably still closes, but it squeaks, sticks, or doesn't align perfectly.
  • "My morning routine is out of whack" — not a disaster, but things aren't going in their usual smooth order.

This nuance makes it a very useful idiom because real life often involves problems that are not total failures — just things that are "off."

QuestionAnswer
  • Core meaning: Something is broken, not functioning right, or out of balance.
  • Origin: American English, late 1800s; from "in whack" meaning in proper working order.
  • What it describes: Machines, body parts, systems, schedules, finances, relationships, numbers.
  • Register: Informal and conversational.
  • Severity: Can be mild or serious — context decides.
  • Key feeling: Things are "off" — not quite right, not working as they should.
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine a friend says:

"Ever since I changed jobs, everything in my life has gone out of whack. My sleep is out of whack, my eating habits are out of whack, and my finances are completely out of whack too."

This tells you clearly: the change in job has disturbed the balance and normal functioning of several important areas of that person's life. Nothing is working as smoothly or as well as it used to.

That is exactly what "out of whack" means — and now you know it completely.
11681:
Imagine a tall tree. The trunk is the thick, strong center. The limbs are the large branches that grow outward from the trunk. Now picture yourself climbing that tree and crawling further and further away from the trunk, toward the thin, fragile end of a branch.

The further out you go, the more dangerous your position becomes. The branch gets thinner, weaker, and more likely to snap. You are far from the safety of the trunk. You can't easily get back. If the branch breaks, you fall — and nobody is there to catch you.

That image of being alone, exposed, and in a risky position is the heart of this idiom.

When someone is "out on a limb," it means they are in a vulnerable or risky position, usually because they:

  • Said or did something bold that others might not agree with or support, OR
  • Took a risk — in a decision, a prediction, a business, or a relationship — without a guarantee of safety or support.

The key feelings baked into this idiom are:

  • Isolation — you are alone in your position, without backup.
  • Vulnerability — you could be proven wrong, embarrassed, or hurt.
  • Risk — things could go badly.
  • Courage — it takes guts to go out on a limb, so the phrase often carries a hint of respect.

Think of it this way:

Going out on a limb = taking a risk where, if things go wrong, you alone face the consequences.

It is the opposite of playing it safe. When you "stay close to the trunk," you are in the safe, comfortable, accepted zone. When you go "out on a limb," you leave that safety behind.

Here are real-life situations where this idiom fits naturally:

1. Making a bold prediction:

"I'm going out on a limb here, but I think our team will win the championship this year."

The speaker knows others might disagree. They are stating something risky, and if it turns out to be wrong, they will look foolish. But they said it anyway.

2. Supporting someone nobody else supports:

"My boss went out on a limb for me when everyone else doubted my abilities."

The boss took a personal risk by supporting this person. If things had gone wrong, the boss would have faced criticism or consequences.

3. Making a risky business decision:

"She went out on a limb and invested all her savings into the startup. Thankfully, it paid off."

She made a bold, risky move with no safety net.

4. Sharing an unpopular opinion:

"I'll go out on a limb and say that the original movie was better than everyone claims."

The speaker knows this view might be met with disagreement or mockery, but they say it anyway.

Use 1 — Taking a risk for yourself

You make a bold choice, a brave prediction, or a daring move — knowing it might fail.

"He went out on a limb and asked for a promotion after only three months on the job."

Use 2 — Taking a risk for someone else

You stick your neck out, vouch for someone, or support them when it costs you something.

"She really went out on a limb for you — you should be grateful."

This second use often carries a tone of debt or gratitude — the person "on the limb" sacrificed their own comfort or safety for you.

This idiom comes from the literal act of climbing trees. When hunters, fruit pickers, or children climbed trees and moved toward the outer tips of branches, they were physically in danger. The branch could crack. There was no support. They were exposed.

The phrase began appearing in American English in the late 1800s, and by the early 20th century it had fully shifted from a literal description into a figurative idiom used in everyday speech, newspapers, and politics.

This idiom is neutral to slightly positive in tone. It doesn't shame someone for being "out on a limb." In fact, it often signals bravery or loyalty. Saying "I'll go out on a limb" before a statement is a humble, honest way of admitting: "I know this is risky, but I believe it enough to say it anyway."

It is not used for reckless or stupid risks. It's used for bold, intentional moves where the person knew the risk and accepted it.

You will almost always see this idiom used with these verbs:

  • "go out on a limb" — the most common form. (I'll go out on a limb and say...)
  • "be out on a limb" — describes someone already in that risky position. (She's really out on a limb with this decision.)
  • "put someone out on a limb" — means to place someone else in a vulnerable position. (You put me out on a limb when you didn't show up.)
  • "leave someone out on a limb" — means to abandon someone who took a risk for you, leaving them exposed. (He left her out on a limb after she defended him publicly.)
Similar Idioms (So You Can Tell the Difference)

These idioms are related but have slight differences:

  • "Stick your neck out" — Very similar. Means to take a risk or speak up when you don't have to. Slightly more emphasis on the act of speaking up than on the isolation.
  • "Take a leap of faith" — Taking a risk based on hope or trust, not evidence. Less about isolation, more about uncertainty.
  • "Put all your eggs in one basket" — Putting everything into one risky option. More about bad strategy than bold courage.
  • "On thin ice" — Being in a situation where one wrong move could cause disaster. Similar danger, but more about imminent threat than personal risk-taking.

"Out on a limb" is unique because it combines personal exposure + isolation + voluntary risk all at once.

"Out on a limb" means you have placed yourself — or someone has placed themselves — in a risky, exposed, and often lonely position, by saying something bold, making a daring decision, or supporting someone when no one else would. If things go wrong, there is no safety net and no one to share the blame. It takes courage to go there.

The next time you hear someone say "I'll go out on a limb here..." — you'll know they're about to say something brave, risky, or bold, and they know it.
11682:
An outbreak is the sudden beginning and rapid spread of something harmful — something that affects not just one person or place, but many people or a large area, usually in a short amount of time.

Think of it this way: imagine a fire that was smoldering quietly inside a building, and then suddenly it bursts through the walls and starts spreading everywhere. That moment of bursting out and spreading — that is the essence of the word outbreak. Something that was small, contained, or hidden suddenly "breaks out" and becomes a wider, dangerous event.
The three key qualities of an outbreak

Every true outbreak has these three features:

  1. Suddenness — It begins abruptly, without much warning. It isn't something that builds slowly over years; it appears and starts spreading quickly.
  2. Spread — It doesn't stay in one spot. It moves — to more people, more places, more areas.
  3. Harm — Almost always, an outbreak involves something dangerous or bad. The word carries a strong sense of alarm and urgency.

1. Diseases and illness — This is the most common use of the word. When a disease suddenly appears and starts infecting many people in a place, we call it an outbreak.

An outbreak of cholera was reported in the flood-affected villages.
Health officials rushed to control the measles outbreak at the school.

The key thing here is that the disease wasn't just present — it suddenly spread, reaching many people quickly.

2. Violence, conflict, and war — When fighting, riots, or war suddenly erupts and spreads across an area or a country, we call it an outbreak of violence or war.

The outbreak of the First World War shocked the entire world.
A sudden outbreak of violence forced thousands of people to flee their homes.

Notice how saying "the outbreak of war" — rather than simply "the start of war" — gives a stronger feeling of alarm and surprise, as if war was something barely held back that suddenly burst free.

3. Fire — When fires break out suddenly in several places or spread rapidly, the word outbreak is used.

An outbreak of wildfires destroyed large parts of the forest.

4. Other harmful things — The word can also describe sudden, spreading episodes of panic, unrest, or disorder.

An outbreak of panic swept through the crowd.
There was a sudden outbreak of protests across the country.

Very rarely, and it sounds unusual. You might hear phrases like an outbreak of laughter or an outbreak of generosity, but these are used for poetic effect or light humor — the word is borrowed from its negative context to make a playful point. In serious, standard usage, the word is almost always negative and alarming.
The difference between an outbreak, an epidemic, and a pandemic

These three words are closely related, especially when talking about disease, and they describe stages of spread:

  • Outbreak: A sudden occurrence of a disease in a specific location, affecting a group of people. It is the early, localised stage. An outbreak of food poisoning at a restaurant.
  • Epidemic: When an outbreak grows and spreads widely across a larger community, region, or country, affecting a large number of people. An epidemic is a grown-up outbreak. A flu epidemic swept across the northern states.
  • Pandemic: When a disease has spread across multiple countries or the entire world. The COVID-19 pandemic affected nearly every country on Earth.

So the path is: outbreak → epidemic → pandemic, each stage representing wider, more severe spread.

Knowing which words are naturally used alongside outbreak will help you use it confidently:

  • Contain an outbreak — to stop it from spreading further
  • Control an outbreak — to manage and reduce it
  • Prevent an outbreak — to stop it from happening at all
  • A fresh outbreak — a new occurrence after a period of calm
  • A major / severe / serious outbreak — one of large scale or intensity
  • An outbreak of [disease / violence / war / fire / unrest]
  • Disease outbreak, virus outbreak, flu outbreak
  • Outbreak response — the actions taken to deal with an outbreak
Putting it all together — more example sentences

• Scientists are working urgently to understand the cause of the new disease outbreak.
  • The government declared a state of emergency after a fresh outbreak of violence in the capital.
  • Dozens of children fell ill in an outbreak of food poisoning linked to the school canteen.
  • The outbreak of war in 1939 ended the brief period of uneasy peace in Europe.
  • Firefighters battled an outbreak of wildfires that had spread across three districts overnight.
  • A sudden outbreak of protests brought thousands onto the streets.

When you read or hear the word outbreak, it should trigger a feeling of urgency and alarm. It tells you that something dangerous has not just appeared — it has escaped containment and is actively spreading. It is a word that signals a crisis is underway or beginning, and that quick action is needed to stop it.

That feeling of something bursting out, uncontrolled and fast-moving, is the soul of the word.
11683:
An outburst is a sudden, forceful release of something strong — usually an emotion, sound, or intense activity — that comes out quickly, powerfully, and often without much warning or control.

Think of a pressure cooker. Steam builds up inside, and at some point it bursts out all at once. An outburst works on the same idea: something — usually a feeling — has been building up inside a person (or building up in a situation), and then it suddenly escapes, loudly and forcefully.

The word is most commonly used for emotions, but it works for several other things too.

1. Emotions
This is where you'll see the word most. Any strong feeling that suddenly comes out can be called an outburst.

  • An outburst of anger — when someone suddenly yells, shouts, or reacts furiously
  • An outburst of laughter — when someone bursts into loud, uncontrollable laughter
  • An outburst of tears — a sudden wave of heavy crying
  • An outburst of joy — a sudden, excited expression of happiness
  • An outburst of grief — a sudden moment of intense sadness

2. Sound or Noise

  • An outburst of noise from the crowd — when a crowd suddenly erupts into loud noise
  • An outburst of cheering — a sudden, collective cheer

3. Intense Activity or Events

  • An outburst of violence — a sudden surge of violent incidents in a place
  • An outburst of creative energy — a sudden, powerful period of creative work
  • An outburst of productivity — a sudden burst of getting a lot done

4. Natural or Scientific Phenomena

  • An outburst of solar energy — scientists use the word for sudden releases of energy from stars or other sources
The Four Core Qualities of an Outburst

These qualities are almost always present when you use this word:

① Sudden — it happens fast, without much build-up or warning. You don't see a slow, gradual process. It hits all at once.

② Intense and forceful — it's strong. An outburst is never mild. A small, quiet sigh is not an outburst. A sudden angry shout is.

③ Brief — it doesn't last long. An outburst is a short burst of something powerful, not a long, continuous state. A person who stays angry all day hasn't had an outburst; a person who suddenly explodes for a minute and then calms down has.

④ Often uncontrolled — the person usually didn't plan it. It's something that just came out — they may not have even wanted it to. This is why outbursts often feel raw and honest, but also sometimes embarrassing or inappropriate.

The word is mostly used in neutral-to-negative contexts, but it isn't strictly a bad word.

When it's negative, it suggests someone lost control in an unwanted way:

His outburst during the meeting embarrassed everyone in the room.

When it's positive or neutral, it simply describes something sudden and powerful that happened:

There was an outburst of laughter when the comedian told the first joke.
The team's victory caused an outburst of joy throughout the city.

So the emotional weight of the word depends on what is bursting out. An outburst of joy feels different from an outburst of rage — but both are still sudden, intense, and brief.
How "Outburst" Sounds — the Feeling of the Word

When a writer or speaker uses the word "outburst," they are usually suggesting:

  • Something that was being held in or held back, and then couldn't be anymore
  • Something that surprised people around it
  • Something that was too strong to be contained in the usual, polite way

Because of this, calling something an "outburst" often hints that it was slightly beyond what was expected in that situation. It's not just "he expressed anger" — it's "he had an outburst of anger," meaning it was sharper, more sudden, and perhaps more unrestrained than normal.
Common Ways You'll See It Used

Here are natural patterns that appear frequently:

  • "an outburst of [emotion/activity]" — the most common structure
  • "have an outburst" — used for people: She had an outburst during the argument.
  • "sudden outburst" — reinforces the unexpected nature
  • "emotional outburst" — a general term for any strong emotional release
  • "angry outburst" — specifically for rage or fury
  • "public outburst" — when it happens in front of others, often drawing attention

The child had a sudden outburst of tears when he dropped his ice cream.

(Sudden, emotional, brief — the classic use.)

There was a loud outburst of applause when the singer finished the song.

(Positive, from a crowd, sudden and powerful.)

Nobody expected his outburst in the middle of the speech — he just started shouting.

(Negative, uncontrolled, caught everyone off guard.)

An outburst of violence followed the controversial announcement.

(Applied to events rather than a single person.)

She tried to stay calm, but an outburst of laughter escaped before she could stop it.

(The "bursting out" quality — she couldn't hold it in.)
How It Differs from Similar Words

Outburst vs. Tantrum — A tantrum is specifically used for children (or childlike behavior in adults) and involves extended crying, screaming, and demands. An outburst is shorter, more sudden, and can apply to anyone.

Outburst vs. Explosion (of emotion) — Both are used similarly, but "explosion" is more figurative and dramatic. "Outburst" is more everyday and specifically implies a short burst, while an "explosion of anger" can feel larger in scale.

Outburst vs. Fit (a fit of rage/laughter) — Very similar in meaning. "Fit" suggests something slightly more prolonged and overpowering; an "outburst" is usually sharper and briefer. Both are informal and commonly used.

Outburst vs. Eruption — "Eruption" (like a volcano) is more dramatic and often implies things building up over a long time before exploding. "Outburst" is the more commonly used, everyday word for similar situations.
An outburst is a short, sudden, powerful release of something strong — especially an emotion — that happens quickly and is often hard to control or predict.
11684:
An outcast is a person who has been pushed out of a group, a community, or a society — and is no longer accepted, welcomed, or treated as a belonging member of that group.

Picture a group of people standing in a circle. The outcast is the person who has been pushed outside that circle and is not allowed back in. They still exist. They may even physically live nearby. But to the group, they no longer belong.
The two sides of being an outcast

Being an outcast involves two things happening at once:

Rejection from others. The group actively refuses to accept the person. They may ignore them, avoid them, treat them with contempt, mock them, or formally ban them. The exclusion comes from the outside — from other people.

Loss of belonging. The outcast is now cut off from the warmth, connection, support, and identity that comes from being part of a group. They must live without the sense of I belong here.

Both of these happen together. A person doesn't simply choose to walk away — they are pushed out, and then they must live with the consequences of that.
Why does someone become an outcast?

There is no single cause. People can become outcasts for many different reasons:

  • Breaking the group's rules or values. Someone who violates the group's moral, religious, or cultural code may be rejected. For example, in certain communities throughout history, someone who married outside their religion, caste, or tribe was cast out.
  • Being different. Sometimes, a person is excluded simply because they are unlike the majority — different beliefs, lifestyle, background, or identity. The group feels threatened or uncomfortable, and pushes the person away.
  • A serious mistake or wrongdoing. Someone who commits a crime, a betrayal, or a deeply shameful act may find that their community no longer wants anything to do with them.
  • Being unfairly blamed. Outcasts are sometimes scapegoats — people who are blamed for a group's problems even if they did nothing wrong. The group projects its anger or fear onto one person and drives them out.
  • Falling from grace. A person who was once part of a group may lose their standing — through failure, scandal, poverty, or disgrace — and suddenly find themselves excluded from a world they once belonged to.

The common thread in all these situations: the group decides, consciously or through collective behavior, that this person no longer belongs among them.
The experience of being an outcast

Being an outcast is not simply about being alone. Many people choose to be alone and feel perfectly fine. Being an outcast is about being denied belonging — and that is a very different, far more painful thing.

The suffering of an outcast typically involves:

Loneliness. The outcast lacks meaningful, accepted connection with others. They may be surrounded by people and still feel completely alone, because those people have turned away from them.

Stigma. Others may treat the outcast as lesser, dangerous, unclean, or shameful. This stigma can follow the person everywhere they go within that community.

Loss of identity. A huge part of who we are comes from the groups we belong to — our family, religion, culture, neighborhood, workplace. When those are stripped away, a person can feel as though they don't know who they are anymore.

Helplessness. Often, the outcast cannot easily undo their exclusion, no matter how desperately they want to. The door has been shut, and they cannot open it from their side.

This is why "outcast" carries such deep sadness. Humans are social creatures. We are built to belong. To be cast out of a group is to be denied something fundamental to human life.

The word works at many different levels of society:

  • A child excluded from a friend group at school is a social outcast in a tiny community.
  • A person shunned by their entire family is a family outcast.
  • Someone expelled from their religion is a religious outcast.
  • In historical societies with rigid hierarchies, entire categories of people were treated as permanent outcasts — lepers forced to live apart from towns, or people born into the lowest rungs of a caste system who were deemed untouchable by others.
  • In literature and scripture, figures banished from their homeland or people — like Cain in the Bible, exiled criminals, or heroes driven from their tribe — are outcasts on the grandest scale.

The size of the group doesn't change the core meaning. Whether it's a classroom or a civilization, an outcast is someone pushed to the outside and denied belonging.

Not always — but it often feels that way, and it frequently is.

Sometimes an outcast is eventually accepted back into a group: through forgiveness, redemption, a change in circumstances, or a shift in the group's attitude. But in many cases, the exclusion is permanent, lasting a lifetime. In some historical societies, it was even inherited — the children of an outcast were also treated as outcasts.

What makes the word so powerful is that it suggests a kind of finality. "Outcast" doesn't just mean someone is temporarily unpopular or going through a rough patch socially. It suggests a deep, serious removal from one's place in the social world.

Several words seem close to "outcast" but mean something slightly different. Understanding these differences sharpens your grasp of the word:

Loner — A loner chooses to be alone. An outcast is forced to be alone, against their will or wish. The critical difference is choice. A loner prefers solitude; an outcast is denied company.

Exile — An exile is physically sent away from a place (a country, a city). An outcast may still physically live among the group but is treated as if they don't exist or don't belong. Exile is about geography; outcast is about belonging. (Though a person can be both — physically exiled and treated as an outcast.)

Pariah — Very similar to "outcast," but pariah specifically emphasizes being treated as contaminated or dangerous — as if mere contact with this person would taint others. An outcast is a broader, more general term. A pariah is an outcast at the extreme end: someone actively avoided, almost as though they carry a disease of shame.

Reject — A "reject" (as a noun) is someone who has been found unworthy or turned away. It is similar, but "outcast" implies deeper, more complete social exclusion. "Reject" is sometimes more casual or narrower in scope; "outcast" suggests a more total removal from a community.

Misfit — A misfit is someone who doesn't fit in, but the focus is on incompatibility — the person simply doesn't match the group's culture. A misfit may feel awkward and out of place, but they haven't necessarily been actively pushed out. An outcast has been rejected; a misfit may just be different.
The tone and feeling of the word

"Outcast" is never a neutral word. It is always emotionally heavy.

When you use the word "outcast," you are not simply describing someone's social status — you are acknowledging that they have experienced a form of exclusion that carries real suffering. The word almost always comes with a sense of sadness, tragedy, or injustice, even in cases where the group believed their rejection was justified.

This is why outcasts appear so often in great literature, religion, mythology, and film. They represent something universally human: the fear of not belonging, of being unwanted, of being invisible to the people around you. The story of the outcast is one of the oldest and most resonant stories in human culture — because deep down, almost every person has, at some point in their life, stood on the edge of a circle wondering whether they truly belong inside it.

• "After the scandal broke, he became an outcast in the small town where he had lived for thirty years — neighbors who once waved to him now crossed the street to avoid him."
  • "As a child who loved books and disliked sports, she always felt like an outcast among her classmates."
  • "The novel follows an outcast from his tribe who must survive alone in an unfamiliar land."
  • "Even after serving his sentence, he returned home to find that the community still treated him as an outcast."
  • "She had been an outcast from her family for years, but she eventually built a new community of people who accepted her completely."

After all of the above, here is the cleanest, most accurate way to say what "outcast" means:

An outcast is a person who has been rejected and excluded by a group or society, and who now lives without the belonging, acceptance, or standing that membership in that group once provided — or that they have always been denied.

Every layer explored above lives inside that definition.
11685:
An outcome is the final result that comes from a situation, process, event, action, or decision. It is what ultimately happens — or what you end up with — after everything plays out.

Think of it like this: something starts, a series of things happen, and then it's over. Whatever you're left with at the end — that's the outcome.

The team worked hard all season. The outcome was a championship win.

The word carries a subtle but important idea: there was uncertainty before it happened. When you use "outcome," you're implying that things could have gone differently. The result wasn't guaranteed. There were multiple possible paths, and this is the one that materialized.

This is why you'll often hear it paired with words like likely, possible, expected, unexpected, best, worst, desired, or potential — because all of those words point to the idea that several different outcomes were on the table before the situation concluded.

Doctors were unsure about the patient's condition. Fortunately, the outcome was a full recovery.
No one knew how the trial would end. The outcome surprised everyone.
The Neutral Nature of the Word

"Outcome" itself has no built-in positive or negative meaning. It simply refers to what happened. Whether the outcome is good or bad depends entirely on the situation and context.

The outcome of the surgery was tragic. (negative)
The outcome of years of practice was mastery. (positive)
The outcome of the vote was a tie. (neutral)

"Outcome" is used across many fields, and knowing this will help you recognize it everywhere:

  • Medicine & Health: Doctors talk about patient outcomes — whether a treatment worked, whether someone recovered, or how their health changed after a procedure. "Studies show better outcomes for patients who exercise regularly."
  • Law & Justice: Courts and cases produce outcomes — someone is found guilty or innocent, a settlement is reached, a case is dismissed. "The outcome of the lawsuit was in the company's favor."
  • Education: Teachers and schools talk about learning outcomes — what students actually learned or are able to do after a course. "The expected outcome of this lesson is that students can solve basic equations."
  • Business & Negotiations: Deals, meetings, and strategies all produce outcomes. "The outcome of the merger negotiations was a new agreement."
  • Research & Science: Studies are conducted and their outcomes tell us what the data revealed. "The outcome of the experiment supported the hypothesis."
  • Sports: Matches and games end in outcomes — wins, losses, or draws. "The outcome of the final match was determined in the last second."
  • Everyday Life: You can use it for any situation where something ends with a result. "I'm nervous about the interview. I hope the outcome is good."
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but each has its own angle:

  • Result — Nearly identical to "outcome," but "result" is more neutral and everyday. It doesn't as strongly imply prior uncertainty. You can say "the result of 2 + 2 is 4" — a fixed, known answer — but saying "the outcome of 2 + 2" would feel odd, because there was never any uncertainty. Outcome is better for situations where things could have gone another way.
  • Consequence — Emphasizes that something caused the result, and often carries a negative or serious tone. "He lied, and now he must face the consequences." Consequences are also often plural and ongoing — they ripple outward. An outcome is more of a single, final endpoint.
  • Effect — Focuses on the direct impact one thing has on another. It's more about cause-and-effect mechanics than about an ending. "The effect of the drug was drowsiness" — that's a specific impact. An outcome is broader and more final.
  • Conclusion — Refers to the end of a reasoning process, a discussion, or a piece of writing. It's not really about what happened in the world, but about what was decided or reasoned. "She came to the conclusion that he was right."
Common Phrases and Patterns You'll See

• "The outcome of [something]" — the most common structure. The outcome of the election. The outcome of the experiment. The outcome of our conversation.
  • "A positive/negative/successful/poor outcome" — attaching a judgment to it.
  • "A likely/possible/potential/expected outcome" — highlighting uncertainty or prediction.
  • "Achieve an outcome" — to successfully reach a desired end result.
  • "Regardless of the outcome" — meaning no matter what happens at the end.
  • "In the best-case/worst-case outcome" — imagining possible scenarios.
One Clean Way to Remember It

Outcome = what you come out with at the end.

The word almost pictures itself: you go into a situation, things unfold, and you come out of it with something — a result, a new state, a changed reality. That "something you come out with" is the outcome.
11686:
An outcrop is a mass of rock that is visible at the surface of the Earth — rock that has broken through or been uncovered, so you can actually see and touch it, rather than it being hidden under layers of soil, grass, or sand.

Think of the Earth's surface as a thick blanket of soil and sediment covering the solid rock beneath. Most of the time, that rock stays buried and invisible. But in certain places, the blanket is thin, torn away, or missing entirely — and there the rock peeks out. That exposed rock, sitting right there on the surface, is an outcrop.

Outcrops can be almost any size or shape. A small one might just be a rocky patch on the ground the size of a table. A large one could be an entire cliff face, a ridge of jagged rock running across a hillside, or a field scattered with boulders and rock slabs. They are often irregular and rough, though some are smooth and flat. Their color depends on what type of rock they are — grey granite, reddish sandstone, dark basalt, and so on. You have almost certainly seen outcrops before, even if you didn't know the word for them.

The main reason outcrops exist is erosion — the slow, natural process by which wind, rain, rivers, glaciers, and ocean waves wear away and carry off soil and softer material over long periods of time. When enough of the overlying material is stripped away, the hard rock beneath is left standing exposed. This is especially common on:

  • Hillsides and mountain slopes, where gravity and rainfall pull soil downward
  • Riverbanks and valley walls, where flowing water carves away the land
  • Coastlines, where waves eat into the shore and reveal rock beneath
  • Desert landscapes, where there's very little vegetation or soil to cover the rock in the first place
  • Hilltops and ridgelines, where wind and rain erode soil over thousands of years

Outcrops can also appear where the land has been cut into by humans — road construction, quarrying, or mining often slices through hills and exposes rock that was previously buried. These are sometimes called artificial outcrops or man-made outcrops.

Sometimes the rock itself is pushed upward from below due to the immense forces inside the Earth (tectonic activity). Over millions of years, rock that was once deep underground can rise to the surface and become exposed.

Outcrops are enormously important to geologists — scientists who study the Earth. Because most rock is buried and inaccessible, outcrops act like natural windows into the Earth's interior. By examining an outcrop, a geologist can determine what type of rock it is, how old it is, how it was formed (whether by volcanic activity, by being compressed under great pressure, or by particles of sediment settling and hardening over time), and what events the Earth went through in that location millions or billions of years ago. In this sense, outcrops are like pages in the Earth's history book.

Outcrops are also studied in mining and mineral exploration, because they can indicate what resources might lie below the surface. If a certain type of rock known to contain gold, copper, or iron ore is spotted in an outcrop, miners know there could be more of it underground.

In less formal or non-geological contexts, "outcrop" is sometimes used figuratively to describe anything that suddenly appears or sticks out from a larger, mostly hidden body. For example, someone might write about "an outcrop of old traditions surviving in a modern city" or "outcrops of violence in an otherwise peaceful region." The metaphor comes directly from the geological meaning — something hidden below the surface emerging into visibility. This figurative use is far less common than the geological one, but you may encounter it in writing.

• The geologist knelt beside the outcrop to examine the rock's layers.
  • Hikers rested on a large granite outcrop overlooking the valley.
  • Erosion had exposed several outcrops of limestone along the river's edge.
  • The map showed a series of sandstone outcrops running along the ridge.

In summary: An outcrop is simply rock that has been exposed at the Earth's surface, visible and accessible rather than buried. It exists because overlying soil and softer material has been worn away, pushed aside, or cut through — leaving bare rock standing out in the open. It is one of the most important things a geologist looks for, because it offers a direct, physical view of what the Earth is made of in that place.
11687:
Imagine a vast layer of rock sitting underground. Now imagine that layer being pushed upward — or the soil around it being worn away by rain and wind over thousands of years — until a portion of that rock breaks through the surface and becomes visible. That exposed, protruding portion of rock is called an outcropping.

In the simplest terms: an outcropping is a mass of rock that sticks up or out from the surrounding ground or hillside, like the tip of something much larger hiding beneath.

Think of a grassy hillside. Most of the hill is covered with soil, grass, and trees. But in one spot, a jagged chunk of dark grey rock juts out of the slope — rough, exposed, bare. That's an outcropping.

Or think of a desert landscape where you see enormous flat-topped rock formations rising dramatically from the sandy ground, with their lower layers buried but their upper portions sticking out boldly. Those are outcroppings.

The key visual idea is always something beneath the surface breaking through and becoming visible above it.

Two main things cause outcroppings to form:

  1. Erosion — Rain, rivers, and wind gradually strip away the soil and softer material on top, slowly revealing the harder rock underneath. Since rock is much tougher than soil, it survives the erosion while everything around it gets worn down.
  2. Geological pressure — Deep underground forces push rock layers upward over millions of years until they poke through the surface.
How is it different from just "a rock"?

A rock sitting on the ground is simply a loose rock. An outcropping is connected to the bedrock beneath — it is part of a continuous underground rock layer or mass. It is not a separate object; it is the visible part of something much bigger that is mostly hidden underground. This is an important distinction.

The word is most commonly used in:

  • Geology and earth science — Scientists study outcroppings to understand what types of rock exist underground without having to dig.
  • Hiking, mountaineering, and nature writing — Describing rocky terrain, cliff faces, and mountain landscapes.
  • Mining and oil exploration — Outcroppings can reveal what minerals or resources might lie deeper underground.
  • Architecture and landscaping — Rock outcroppings are sometimes incorporated into garden designs or building sites.

Like many concrete words in English, "outcropping" is also used figuratively — that is, metaphorically — to describe anything that is a visible sign or small emergence of something larger and mostly hidden.

For example:

  • "The argument was just an outcropping of deeper resentments that had been building for years."
    Here, the argument is like the exposed rock — the visible part of a much bigger, hidden problem below the surface.
  • "Small outcroppings of resistance began to appear across the country."
    Meaning: small, visible signs of a broader, underlying resistance that was growing.

The figurative sense always preserves the same logic: a small, visible portion of something that is much larger and mostly unseen or hidden beneath the surface.

You will often see both "outcropping" and "outcrop" used to mean the same thing. Outcrop is slightly more common in strict geological writing, while outcropping tends to appear more in everyday and literary contexts. Treat them as interchangeable — they refer to the same thing.

• The geologist examined the limestone outcropping on the side of the canyon.
  • Hikers rested on a flat granite outcropping that offered a clear view of the valley.
  • The construction crew had to blast through a large outcropping before they could lay the road.
  • Her brief smile was a small outcropping of the warmth she rarely showed anyone.

An outcropping is a mass of rock that has broken through the earth's surface and is now visibly sticking out from the surrounding ground — the exposed, protruding face of an otherwise buried rock layer — and by extension, any small, visible sign of a larger hidden thing.
11688: An outcry is a strong, loud expression of anger, protest, or shock — usually from many people at once — in reaction to something that feels wrong, unfair, or deeply troubling. Think of it as the collective voice of people who are upset and want to be heard.
The Two Senses of the Word

Outcry has two senses: one literal and one figurative. The figurative one is by far the more common in modern English.

The literal sense means an actual, audible cry — a shout of alarm, pain, or shock. For example: "There was an outcry from the stadium crowd when the goalkeeper was knocked unconscious." Here, people are physically crying out. This sense is older and less frequently used today.

The figurative sense — the one you will encounter most often — refers to a wave of strong public reaction against something. It doesn't involve actual screaming, but the emotion is just as intense. It is the kind of reaction where many people, together, express their anger or disapproval loudly and persistently. For example: "The government's decision to cut hospital funding sparked a nationwide outcry." Nobody is literally shouting, but the public is making a lot of noise through protests, social media, petitions, speeches, interviews, and demonstrations.
What Makes Something an "Outcry" and Not Just Criticism

This is important. Not every complaint or disagreement is an outcry. The word carries specific qualities that set it apart:

It is intense. An outcry is not mild displeasure or a quiet frown of disapproval. It is fuelled by strong emotion — outrage, indignation, moral shock. When people feel something is deeply wrong or unjust, that is when an outcry happens.

It is usually collective. A single person complaining is not an outcry. The word strongly suggests a group — often a large group — reacting together. This is why you will so often see it paired with the word "public," as in "public outcry." That phrase means that ordinary people, broadly and widely, are expressing strong disapproval.

It is reactive. An outcry doesn't appear out of nowhere. Something triggers it — a decision, an event, a revelation, a scandal, an injustice. The outcry is the response to that trigger.

It implies the reaction is justified, or at least understandable. When a writer uses the word "outcry," there is usually a quiet suggestion that the people reacting have a good reason to be upset. It gives the protest a sense of legitimacy.
How the Word Is Actually Used

Knowing how "outcry" is used in real sentences is just as important as knowing the definition. Here are the patterns you'll most commonly see:

"Public outcry" is the most frequent combination. "The new law caused a public outcry." The word "public" tells you the anger is widespread, not limited to one group.

"Widespread outcry" is similar. It emphasizes that the reaction extends across many different places or communities.

Outcry is often "caused," "sparked," "triggered," or "provoked" by something. These verbs all point to the idea that an event sets it off. "The CEO's pay raise sparked an outcry among employees."

Outcry can also be described as happening "amid" or "in the face of" something. "The company proceeded with its plans amid widespread outcry." This means the company ignored the protest and moved ahead anyway.

Outcry is very often followed by "over" or "against." "There was an outcry over the proposed demolition of the historic building." / "An outcry against the new tax policy grew louder each day."
Concrete Examples to Cement Your Understanding

Imagine a beloved park in a city is going to be torn down to build a parking lot. Residents, environmentalists, and local historians are furious. They write letters, hold protests, post on social media, and appear on the news demanding the plan be stopped. This collective anger and protest is an outcry — specifically, a public outcry against the destruction of the park.

Imagine a famous athlete is caught cheating in a competition. Fans, sports commentators, fellow athletes, and the media are all reacting with disbelief and anger. The reaction that follows — the flood of angry opinions, the demand for consequences, the sense of moral betrayal felt by millions — is an outcry.

Now imagine a quieter scenario: a child stumbles and falls at a playground. Another child nearby lets out a gasp and cries out in alarm. That sudden, audible cry is also an outcry — in its more literal, physical sense.

When you read or hear the word "outcry," it should immediately signal to you that something significant has happened and people are not staying quiet about it. It carries a sense of urgency, of moral weight, of people who feel they cannot and will not stay silent. It is a word associated with justice, protest, and collective conscience. It is rarely used for trivial things. When something provokes an outcry, it means it has genuinely disturbed or angered a large number of people.

Complaint is calm and formal. You file a complaint. An outcry is emotional and urgent — you don't file an outcry, you cause one or spark one.

Protest is close in meaning, but a protest is often a planned, organized action (like a march or demonstration). An outcry can be spontaneous and unorganized — it is the raw reaction before any formal protest is even planned.

Uproar and furore are very close synonyms. The slight difference is that "outcry" often emphasizes the sense of moral outrage and the voices of real people, while "uproar" emphasizes the chaotic noise and disorder, and "furore" is often used for short-lived but intense media or public controversy.

Criticism is intellectual and measured. An outcry is emotional and collective. You can criticize something calmly and alone; an outcry requires intensity and usually numbers.

"Outcry" is a neutral-to-formal word. It fits naturally in news reporting, academic writing, formal essays, and serious conversation. It is not slang, and it is not overly technical. You will regularly see it in newspapers, political discussions, social commentary, and literature.

If you had to capture everything above in one sentence, it would be this: an outcry is a strong, emotional reaction — usually of anger or protest — from many people together, triggered by something they feel is wrong, unfair, or shocking, expressed so loudly and persistently that it cannot be ignored.
11689:
Something is outdated when it was once current, useful, or accepted — but is no longer so, because the world has moved on. It belongs to a past moment that has now been replaced by something newer, more accurate, or more suitable.

The key idea is a mismatch with the present. The thing itself hasn't necessarily broken or disappeared — it just no longer fits now.

Think of it this way: "outdated" is built from the idea of being past its date — like a deadline that's already passed. Something outdated has, in a sense, expired its relevance.

It always implies a comparison between then (when it was fine) and now (when it isn't). Without that contrast, the word doesn't apply.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Outdated?

Almost anything can be outdated — and understanding this range is essential:

Information and knowledge
If a textbook says the population of a country is 80 million, but the actual population is now 130 million, that information is outdated. It was once correct. Now it misleads.

Technology
A floppy disk is outdated. It was once the standard way to store and transfer files. Computers no longer even have slots for them. Using one today is impractical — not because it's broken, but because the world has moved to USB drives, cloud storage, and beyond.

Methods and practices
Doctors once used to bleed patients (literally cut them and drain blood) to cure illness. That method is outdated — completely replaced by better medical understanding.

Laws and rules
Some countries still have laws on their books that were written centuries ago. Those laws may be outdated — written for a reality that no longer exists.

Ideas and beliefs
The idea that the Earth is the centre of the universe was once widely believed. It is now an outdated belief — overturned by science.

Design and style
A website built in the late 1990s — with flashing text, tiled backgrounds, and giant buttons — looks visually outdated today, because design standards have evolved completely.

Software
If you're running an old version of an app that no longer receives updates, it is outdated — it may have security vulnerabilities, missing features, and poor compatibility with modern systems.
The Spectrum: How "Outdated" Relates to Other Words

This is crucial for a learner. Several words sit near "outdated," but they are not identical.

Old is neutral. A 100-year-old painting is old, but it isn't outdated — it wasn't made to be "current." "Old" simply describes age.

Outdated carries a sense of failure to keep up. It implies something should be current or was once current, but has fallen behind.

Obsolete is stronger than outdated. When something is obsolete, it is not just behind — it is completely out of use. No one uses it anymore. The VCR is arguably obsolete. An outdated thing can often still be used (awkwardly or poorly); an obsolete thing typically cannot be used at all in practical terms.

Old-fashioned tends to be used more for style, attitude, or social customs — and often carries a warmer or more nostalgic tone. "He has old-fashioned manners" is not a harsh criticism. "Outdated" is more neutral-to-negative, and more commonly applied to facts, systems, and technology.

Stale is used specifically for information or content that was once fresh and current but has gone dry — like stale news or stale data.

"Outdated" is mildly negative, but not harshly so. It doesn't insult — it simply identifies a gap between what is and what should be for the present time.

When someone says your thinking is outdated, they mean your ideas haven't kept pace with what is now known or accepted. It's a criticism, but a factual one rather than a personal attack.

When you say a machine is outdated, you're saying: it works, perhaps, but it's no longer the right tool for today's world.

"Outdated" sits comfortably in two positions in a sentence:

Before the noun (attributive position):
"This is an outdated map."
"We're using outdated equipment."

After a linking verb (predicative position):
"This map is outdated."
"The equipment feels outdated."
"The policy has become outdated."

Both are natural and common. The word works smoothly in either place.

Certain words pair with "outdated" so often that knowing them will help you recognise and use the word naturally:

  • outdated information / data / statistics — facts that are no longer current
  • outdated technology / software / hardware / systems — tools that have been surpassed
  • outdated methods / practices / procedures — ways of doing things that have been replaced
  • outdated laws / regulations / policies — rules made for a different time
  • outdated ideas / beliefs / views / thinking — concepts that no longer hold up
  • outdated design / interface / look — visual styles that no longer feel current
  • become outdated / grow outdated — to describe the process of falling behind over time
  • quickly outdated / rapidly outdated — used when something loses currency very fast (e.g., technology)

The natural opposites of "outdated" are:

  • Current — reflects the present moment
  • Up-to-date — has been updated to match the present
  • Modern — belongs to or suits the present era
  • Relevant — applies meaningfully to the present situation
  • Contemporary — existing or occurring in the same time as now

These are designed to show the word in real, natural use:

  1. "The company's website looks outdated — it hasn't been redesigned since 2005."
  2. "Her research is built on outdated data; the figures she's using are from fifteen years ago."
  3. "That approach to teaching is outdated; modern educators now know that memorisation alone isn't effective."
  4. "The GPS in his old car was so outdated that it was still showing roads that had been demolished years ago."
  5. "Some of the safety rules in this factory are outdated and need to be revised."
  6. "He held some outdated views on gender roles that made conversations awkward."
  7. "The phone wasn't broken — it was simply outdated, unable to run any of the newer apps."

Imagine a calendar on a wall. The year shown is 2010. The calendar is perfectly intact — not damaged, not wrong in its own terms. But it is outdated because it no longer tells you anything useful about today. It served its purpose then. It doesn't now.

That gap — between what was once right and what is needed now — is the heart of "outdated."
